title: Ad attribution is one view of the customer journey, not the whole business picture
argument: Use direct attribution to understand what it can show, and the broader business picture to understand what it may not capture; do not assume either one proves the whole story.
audience: Wedding-business owners evaluating whether their advertising is contributing to inquiries and bookings, especially when some customers enter through other channels.
tension: A business can see some ad-attributed activity and still have bookings whose discovery path is unclear.
take: Use direct attribution to understand what it can show, and the broader business picture to understand what it may not capture; do not assume either one proves the whole story.
mechanism: Whitney proposed including sales, not only booked calls, in future reports and explained that someone might see an ad before later inquiring organically. She framed that journey as a possibility, not an established explanation for the client's untracked bookings.
source_assertions: [moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Whitney proposed including sales as well as booked calls in future reports and cited a reported May Google Ads lead that became a $14,000 Funktastic booking.

[moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Mike said the client's accountant and bookkeeper indicated the business was up about 30% year to date; the passage does not detail the calculation or period boundaries.
[moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Mike said some planner bookings were not in LeadLock and that he did not know how those clients found the business.

[moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Whitney described a possible ad-to-site-to-organic-inquiry journey; Marisa separately said callers often mentioned Instagram and offered her view that they must have seen an ad.
inference: Direct attribution and total business movement can inform different parts of an evaluation, but the conversation does not establish whether advertising caused the wider business increase or the untracked planner bookings.
qualifiers: The booking and business-growth figures were reported in the meeting, not independently verified.

title: A rebrand can reach ad landing pages before the new site is finished

audience: Wedding-business owners refreshing their brand while advertising is active, particularly those deciding whether campaign landing pages must wait for a new website.
tension: A brand refresh and a website build may move on different timelines, while ad traffic still arrives at a landing page.
take: Once brand elements are approved, ad landing pages can be considered as part of the rebrand even while the full website is still being built.

title: A buyer survey and a wedding-day form answer different questions
argument: Ask about the buying decision while it is fresh, and keep that research distinct from the operational questions needed to serve the couple.
audience: Wedding-business owners who want to understand why clients chose them and also gather practical details for planning and service delivery.
tension: One client relationship may create useful marketing insight and important service information, but one questionnaire may not serve both purposes well.
take: Ask about the buying decision while it is fresh, and keep that research distinct from the operational questions needed to serve the couple.
mechanism: Whitney distinguished reviews from direct questions about deciding factors, proposed sending a short research survey shortly after contract signing, and recommended keeping it separate from a pre-wedding planning form. Marisa and Mike described the information they hoped to learn about couples and buyer choices.

[moment_0ced0a098e016faa7be084e1] When Marisa asked about combining research with a pre-wedding form, Whitney recommended treating them as separate tools, with a short post-contract research survey and an operational form in the client's CRM.

title: A monthly creative bank is not a mandate to replace every working ad
argument: Creative refresh timing can respond to campaign performance rather than a fixed monthly swap, and the owner still needs a reliable way to review what changed and why.
audience: Wedding-business owners who want to understand creative-refresh decisions and stay involved in reviewing campaign work.
tension: New content may be ready while current ads are still working, and updates can be hard for a client to follow if they miss informal communication.
take: Creative refresh timing can respond to campaign performance rather than a fixed monthly swap, and the owner still needs a reliable way to review what changed and why.
mechanism: Carmen explained her account-specific approach to retaining working creative and refreshing when performance declined. Marisa asked for a formal review cadence because she sometimes missed updates, and Whitney offered a recurring strategy meeting.
source_assertions: [moment_baa14f0096a2495fb5aa0669] Carmen said new ad creative was available each month but that she generally avoided changing creative she believed was working, refreshed retargeting less often, and refreshed some conversion creative when performance declined.

inference: A useful creative process can include both a reason not to change an ad and a clear client review point; this exchange does not establish that the recurring meeting was scheduled.

title: When local searches are scarce, use the owner's inquiry pattern and a clear review signal
argument: Low search activity is not, by itself, proof that a campaign should stop; assess the owner's inquiry pattern and define what later campaign behavior would warrant a change.
audience: Wedding-business owners testing a niche or adjacent service in a local market where search activity may be limited.
tension: A campaign with impressions but no clicks offers little evidence about what would happen in a busier period, while continued activity would still need a meaningful review point.

title: A lead lull may need a wider diagnosis than Google Ads
argument: When inquiries slow, first establish whether the change is broader than paid ads; if several parts of the journey change at once, a short-lived increase does not identify which one caused it.
audience: Wedding venues and other wedding businesses experiencing a change in inquiries and trying to understand whether it is limited to paid advertising.
tension: The client saw a period with no inquiries across paid and organic, followed by a brief increase after multiple changes and then another lull.
take: When inquiries slow, first establish whether the change is broader than paid ads; if several parts of the journey change at once, a short-lived increase does not identify which one caused it.
mechanism: Fallon asked whether the slowdown was also happening organically, checked LeadLock, used the client's location input to update Google targeting, and identified the page or ads as areas for further review. The client made the landing-page changes.
source_assertions: [moment_a3deaf92e77cc94f7c6548e5] Fallon asked the venue client whether the slowdown was also happening organically; she reported that the lull appeared in both paid and organic activity.
[moment_a3deaf92e77cc94f7c6548e5] The client wanted to focus on more specific locations and supplied them; Fallon said she updated Google targeting, while the client made landing-page changes.
[moment_a3deaf92e77cc94f7c6548e5] Fallon reported that about four leads came in during a week after the changes, then said the most recent lead had been on June 6 and that the lull had returned.

[moment_a3deaf92e77cc94f7c6548e5] Fallon said she lacked enough historical context to know whether the pattern was usual and planned to look further back; Meta had only recently launched and did not yet have enough data in her account.
inference: The exchange supports a broader diagnostic approach but does not establish whether the targeting update, page changes, seasonality, or another factor explains the temporary lead increase or later lull.
qualifiers: Lead counts and timing were reported by Fallon and were not independently verified.
The targeting and landing-page changes occurred together, so their effects cannot be separated from this account.
The transcript does not supply the meeting date or year for the June 6 reference.
The source says historical review was still needed; no final diagnosis or resolution is reported.
The lead counts and timing are reported by Fallon; the transcript does not independently verify them.
The later increase followed changes to both Google locations and the landing page, so the exchange does not isolate a cause.
Meta had only recently launched and was not yet supported by enough data in Fallon's account.
Carmen explicitly said she did not have enough historical context to explain the pattern.
risks: Confirm permission and anonymize the venue and client before sharing account details.
Do not present the temporary increase as a result caused by either change or as a recurring industry pattern.
